1:
The address is read as a deliberate turn away from the men just silenced. Gill places it after the priests and Pharisees had left him nonplussed, and finds two dangers in that moment: the people, having seen their teachers' errors detected, might conclude there was nothing in religion, or, overawed by the authority of men in Moses's chair, might be led by them into bad principles; the discourse guards both, and clears Christ of being an enemy to Moses rightly explained. Wesley reads the opening word the same way, that he left all converse with his adversaries, whom he now left to the hardness of their hearts. Calvin states the design more broadly, that the word of God might remain entire amid the noise of combat, since men are prone to dislike the Law and grow wanton through a dissolute pastor's example, forming their rulers' corrupt manners into a law for themselves; and he notes that the attack is ordered, the Law being first vindicated from contempt before the teachers are exposed. Ellicott hears an appeal to the unperverted conscience of the people against the perversions of their guides, and observes that Christ closes his public teaching as he began it, with a protest against a casuistry that had put the traditions of men in the place of the commandments of God.

The seat itself is defined before the obedience due to it. Lightfoot takes it of the legislative chair rather than the merely doctrinal, so that Christ asserts the authority of the magistrate and bids them obey in lawful things. Henry reads it of the Sanhedrim, the standing bench that determined appeals rather than the judges who rode the circuit, and allows the other application to the scribes who expounded the law, since Ezra's pulpit of wood is here called Moses's seat; he draws two notes from it, that many a good place is filled with bad men, the seat being dishonoured by the men rather than the men honoured by the seat, and that a useful office is not to be abolished because bad men abuse it. Barnes explains the custom, that they sat to expound the law and rose to read it, so that sitting in the seat means authority to teach. Clarke adds the sharper distinction, that they sat there formerly by divine appointment and now by divine permission. Robertson calls it the chair of the professor whose function is to interpret Moses, and quotes the view that they were heirs of his authority by an unbroken tradition.

The command to observe is then limited, and the burden they laid on is disputed. Barnes says the word all cannot stand unrestricted, since Christ himself charges them with teaching against the law and making it void by tradition. Gill restrains it to what agrees with the chair they sit in, many of their glosses being repugnant to the law. Clarke presses the past tense, whatsoever they have commanded, and suggests a reference to a former period when they taught the way of God in truth. Ellicott finds the lack not in the maxims but in the life, it being one thing to draw fine pictures of virtue and another to live by them. Robertson puts it that as teachers they have their place, but their practice is not to be copied. On the burdens Gill and Clarke name the traditions of the elders, added without reason, expediency or revelation, while Barnes argues from the apostle's words at Jerusalem that the rites of Moses must be meant, since Christ would not have bidden the people keep traditions. Calvin denies that harsh laws are in view at all and finds the fault in the stern manner of enforcing them. Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic saying that the crafty wicked man is he who prescribes light things to himself and heavy to others, and Robertson that they are taskmasters, not burden-bearers.
5:
The motive is treated as the root of the whole indictment. Ellicott says our Lord fixes, as in the Sermon on the Mount, on the love of man's applause as the thing that vitiated the highest ethical teaching and the most rigorous outward holiness, and finds a special edge in the fact that many among the chief rulers were convinced of his claims yet afraid to confess him, so that some may have listened knowing he spoke of them. Calvin takes it further, that whatever is apparently good in such men is hypocritical and worthless, the things they boast of being absolute trifles because they spring from mere ostentation, and an upright worshipper never giving himself to that empty parade. Gill observes that their prayers, alms and fastings were all performed in public, so that they sought neither the glory of God nor the good of their fellow creatures nor any pleasure to themselves. Henry grants that we must do good works which those who see them may glorify God for, but not proclaim them that others may glorify us; in the duties that fall under the eye of men none were so abundant, while in the recesses of their hearts they desired to be excused.

The two ornaments are then explained. Barnes derives the name from a word signifying to keep or guard, the things being worn as amulets supposed to defend from evil, and describes the frontlet of four inscribed parchments enclosed in tough skin and bound to the forehead with a thong. Lightfoot gives the Jewish side, the four places of the law written on labels called tephillin and fastened to the forehead and the left arm, the forehead one most conspicuous and so made broad, and quotes the rule that a man may pass a synagogue during prayers if he has them on his head, because they show he is studious of the law. Robertson adds that each strip was to be tied with a well-washed hair from a calf's tail, lest thread or wool breed a growth that would pollute it. Wesley says they supposed them a kind of charm against danger, and notes that the fringes were commanded to remind them of doing all the commandments. Henry reads the original command as figurative, intimating no more than that we should bear the things of God in mind as carefully as if they were bound between our eyes, and distinguishes a gracious ambition to be holier than others from a proud one to appear so.

On the seats and the titles the comment turns partly antiquarian. Barnes says the word rooms misses the original, the guests not sitting but reclining on couches ranged about three sides of a square with the open end toward the servants. Ellicott prefers the first places, nearest the host, and locates the synagogue seats at the upper end where the ark stood, assigned by the elders to those most conspicuous for devotion to the law and so coveted as a mark of religious reputation. Robertson calls it an insatiable hunger for prominence, and recalls that the apostles fell into an ugly quarrel over precedence at the last supper, two days after hearing this. Lightfoot shows the title to be late, the worthier times having had no need of it, since Hillel came up out of Babylon without it and the prophet is named Haggai and not Rabbi Haggai; it began with the presidents of the council. Clarke ranks the three forms as degrees of comparison, rabh great, rabbi greater and rabban greatest, and reports that the second Rabbi is omitted by several good manuscripts and most of the ancient versions. Calvin presses the prohibition hardest, that the honour belongs to Christ alone and cannot be given to a man without injury to him. Henry answers that the places themselves are not condemned, since somebody must sit uppermost.
8:
The turn to the disciples is noticed before the prohibition is weighed. Robertson calls it an apparent aside, with the pronoun thrown forward for emphasis, quotes an old Greek commentator to the effect that one is forbidden to seek the name, not blamed if others use it. Clarke dates the title closely, no prophet having borne it and no Jewish doctor before Hillel and Shammai, whose rival schools had divided the people between two infallible teachers, so that the Pharisees took up a title then newly in vogue and trained their followers to use it. Gill reads the ban as aimed at the thing rather than the word, that they were not to think themselves men of authority with dominion over the faith of others and power to bind consciences at pleasure. Barnes puts the reason positively, that they were brethren on a level and equal in authority, so that nothing was to be done which might lead the world to suppose there were ranks and grades among them. Henry quotes the rabbinic maxim that he who salutes his teacher without calling him Rabbi provokes the divine Majesty to depart from Israel, and answers that respect is commendable in the man who gives it and abominable in the man who demands it.

On father and master the application is pressed home to the church. Ellicott grants the beauty of the word in its true use, where the relation of scholar and teacher was filial on one side and paternal on the other, and says it was dangerous precisely because the idea was noble; he then traces the parallel in Christendom, Abbot from Abba, Papa and Pope risen from a name once given to every priest, and our own Father in God for bishops, while warning that a slavish literalism would be no better. Barnes defines the word by what it carries, authority and eminence and a right to command, which belongs eminently to God, and explains the Jewish appetite for it by the notion that a teacher formed the man and gave him real life. Robertson adds that it was not then a common address to a living person but a title of honour for great men of the past, and declines to read the sentence as forbidding a child his own father. Clarke suspects an allusion to the Ab of the Sanhedrin, and infers that no second after Christ was to be set up in a church of which he alone is head. Calvin refuses to divide the word between flesh and spirit, since an apostle twice calls himself a father, and locates the fault: the honour is falsely ascribed to men when it obscures the glory of God.

Greatness is then redefined as service. Calvin says the conclusion shows that he was not disputing about words after the manner of the sophists but looking at the fact, that the highest honour in the church is not government but service, so that a man who keeps within that limit takes nothing from God whatever title he bears, and asks what it avails that the Pope styles himself a servant while framing laws to oppress souls. Ellicott weighs two senses of the clause, a law of retribution by which the man who grasps at being greatest ends as servant of all, or the law which our Lord's own life best illustrated, that real greatness shows itself in ministration rather than in assertion; he prefers the second. Gill allows both the man who truly is greatest, having more grace and larger gifts, and the man who merely wants to be, and lays down that he who would be most esteemed ought to do the most work. Barnes says that God will honour the man who seeks a lowly place, and Wesley that no sentence of our Lord's is repeated so often, standing with scarcely a variation ten times in the evangelists.
13:
The woes are first weighed as a whole. Henry hears them as claps of thunder from Sinai, set deliberately against the eight beatitudes, and the more dreadful for coming from one who came to bless and loved to bless, since a woe from Christ is a woe without remedy; he adds that hypocrite primarily means a stage-player in religion, a man acting the part of one he neither is nor would be. Wesley reads the same arithmetic but insists on the tone, that these are not imprecations but solemn and compassionate declarations of the misery such stubborn sinners were bringing on themselves. Ellicott doubts our English rendering altogether, since the Greek interjection is capable of sorrow as well as indignation, and suggests woe for you as the better phrase. Barnes calls it the most appalling discourse ever delivered to mortals, spoken in the temple before multitudes and standing as the last of his public teaching. Robertson traces the word hypocrite through its history, from answering to taking a part on the stage, and so by an easy step to feigning and wearing a mask, and notes that this hardest word from the lips of Jesus falls on the religious leaders of the nation. Gill observes that the men addressed had not withdrawn after their confusion but were still about him watching for an advantage.

How many woes there are turns out to be a textual question. Robertson counts seven, the eighth being the verse on widows' houses which the revisers put in the margin as a gloss drawn from the other two Gospels, and notes that the manuscripts which do keep it cannot agree whether it stands before or after this one. Clarke keeps the verse but reverses the order, reporting that the transposition is supported by some of the best manuscripts, versions and fathers, and that the critic whose edition first omitted the verse restored it in the second edition transposed exactly so. Henry, Wesley and Gill all count eight without discussing the evidence, Gill noting that the woe is pronounced no less than eight times and that it expresses abhorrence of their wickedness, commiseration of their case and their certain destruction together.

The charge itself is read as the perversion of an office. Calvin says they are cursed because the government of the church was in their hands and they turned it to the destruction of the people, since doctrine is the door by which men enter life and the keys were committed to pastors for admitting them; from Luke's phrase he gathers that the guardians of the law had robbed the people of its true understanding, and he adds that the Papists forge keys of their own as if these had some magical power apart from the word of God. Ellicott identifies the key as the symbol handed to each scribe on his admission to office, and says the only use they made of it was to lock the door, neither entering into the inner meaning of the Law and the Prophets themselves nor letting in those who were entering. Barnes itemises the means: false teaching about the Messiah, the binding of the people to tradition, and the open argument that Jesus was an impostor, by which many who were on the point of entering were turned back. Henry sets against this what they ought to have done, opened the prophecies that pointed to the Messiah and shown that Daniel's weeks were expiring and the sceptre departed from Judah, whereas they pressed a ceremonial law then vanishing and suppressed the prophecies then being fulfilled; they would not enter because they were too proud to stoop to his meanness, repentance being the door and nothing more disagreeable to men who admired themselves. Gill alone enters a caveat, that what men can shut is not eternal happiness itself, the entrance to which no man opens or shuts.
14:
How the widows were stripped is set out concretely. Barnes takes the word houses for property of any kind and finds two methods, a reputation for exact justice to the poor which induced widows to make them guardians and executors of estates they then defrauded, and an appearance of sanctity which drew gifts from weak women under pretence of religious uses. Ellicott offers the same pair in the terms of the time, that as the jurists and notaries of the day they could press unjust claims against wealthy widows or get themselves made their heirs, and that devout women were taught that the maintenance of a scribe was the best use of wealth. Lightfoot exhibits one of the arguments forged on that anvil, a ruling that because the Lord commanded an ark of shittim wood to be made, the fellow citizens of a disciple of the wise are bound to do his servile work for him; they angled, he says, with a double hook, for respect, and by respect for gain. Gill marks only that the same character is repeated with a fresh reason.

The long prayers are then weighed as the cloak. Calvin says Christ does not merely charge them with open crimes but tears away the disguise of a virtue, since the holier a man is the more he is given to prayer, so that their case is the worse: they were so impure that the chief part of the worship of God could not be used by them without sin, and they sold their prayers as hirelings dispose of their daily labour. Henry refuses to let the censure fall on length itself, since the cloak must be thick that could cover such practices and Christ himself continued a whole night in prayer; what he condemns is a stated form said over by tale and used for a pretence, so that while they seemed to soar heavenward their eye was on some widow's house that lay convenient, and he adds that the plea which disguises sin now will aggravate the condemnation, there being degrees of damnation. Barnes reports that their devotions ran to three hours, and Ellicott identifies them more precisely with the standard series of eighteen prayers.

The hunt for converts is read as the same greed under another form. Ellicott recalls that the zeal of the earlier Pharisees had been a propagandism closer to the spread of the religion of Mahomet than of the gospel, John Hyrcanus having offered the Idumeans death, exile or circumcision, and that when Rome made force impossible they fell back on persuasion and exulted over a single heathen enrolled. Barnes distinguishes the two classes, the proselyte of righteousness who was circumcised and kept the whole law and the proselyte of the gate who renounced the pagan rites without being circumcised, and says the Pharisees sought them to swell their numbers or to extort their money, taking no pains afterwards to instruct or restrain them. Robertson narrows the charge, that what was made was a convert to Pharisaism rather than to Judaism, few even of the full proselytes becoming Pharisees, and judges the effort a comparative failure whose successes were worse than its failures. Clarke treats the opening phrase as proverbial, like leaving no stone unturned, reports that the word rendered twofold has been shown to mean rather more deceitful, and glosses son of hell as one who might claim hell for his mother. Lightfoot quotes the rabbis against their own converts, that proselytes hinder the coming of the Messiah and are as a scab to Israel, which Barnes and Ellicott both repeat; yet, he says, the more they could draw over, the more purses there were to fish in. Calvin grants the work would have been holy in itself, but to bring strangers into a worship by then degenerate was to hurry them from one danger into a greater.
16:
The new title is noticed before the casuistry is examined. Robertson points out that this third woe drops the usual address altogether and that the name blind guides had already been used of them earlier in the Gospel. Wesley reads the change of title as deliberate, the first naming their personal character and the second their influence upon others. Gill says the men who professed to guide the blind were blind themselves, ignorant of God in Christ, of the true Messiah and of the spirituality of the law, their minds darkened by an insatiable covetousness. Henry finds it sad that so many should be under the guidance of men who undertake to show others a way they are themselves willingly ignorant of, and recalls the prophet's watchmen who are blind while the people love to have it so. Calvin states the mechanism, that the world has a natural propensity to error but that improper modes of worship gain a footing only when those in authority confirm them, such men not merely conniving at errors which are a source of gain to them but helping to fan the flame.

What the gold was, and why it was thought to bind, is then settled. Lightfoot identifies it not as the gold shining in the walls and ceilings but as the gold offered in the sacred treasury, and explains the practice: to swear by the temple or by the altar was so common as to be esteemed nothing and thought scarcely binding, whereas a man who swore by the treasury supposed himself tied indispensably. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by reasoning about the casuistry itself, that coin or bullion given to the treasure had received a more special consecration than the fabric, and compares the popular feeling which makes an oath binding only when the Book is kissed, or the later Christendom that found a saint's relics holier than the Gospels. Gill treats the clause as a quotation of their own maxim, an oath by the altar being reckoned either no sin at all or no obligation, to be kept or broken as a man thought fit.

The reply is read as an argument from the nature of an oath. Barnes puts it as a simple inversion: the gold had no holiness except what the temple gave it, and would be no holier than any other gold elsewhere, so that the greater thing cannot be the one that derives its sanctity from the less; the altar likewise sanctifies the gift, and in the end every man who swears at all swears by God, or his oath is worth nothing. Calvin leads the question back to its source, that it is lawful to swear by no name but God's, so that the temple may be sworn by only as the sanctuary where his glory shines, God permitting himself to be called as witness through such symbols of his presence provided no divinity is ascribed to them. Clarke makes the same point from what an oath presupposes, a witness able to punish perjury, so that whether a man swore by the temple or the gold, the altar or the gift, he had invoked the God of all four, who would punish him even in the cases they had exempted. Wesley spells out what the altar carries with it, not the gift only but the holy fire and the sacrifice, and above all the God to whom these belong, since every oath by a creature is an implicit appeal to him. Gill enters the caution that Christ is not allowing any of these oaths, having forbidden them elsewhere, but telling a man what he has invoked. Robertson observes that the word fools is used here of their stupidity although it had been forbidden in anger, which shows that not the word but the spirit in which it is uttered is what matters.
23:
The tithing of herbs is first placed within the law. Lightfoot gives the general rule as the rabbis state it, that whatever serves for food and grows out of the earth is to be tithed, observes that the tithing of garden herbs was an addition of the scribes which our Saviour nevertheless approved when he said these ought not to have been left undone. Barnes reckons that by law nearly a third of a Jew's property went to religious uses, and identifies the three plants as herbs of little value, the first being strewn on the floors of houses and synagogues for its fragrance. Ellicott notes that the law names only corn and wine and oil among the produce of the earth, so that the gathering of the tenth sprig of every herb rested on a wider phrase elsewhere; done at the bidding of an imperfectly illumined conscience, he says, it is not blamed, since unlike the teaching about oaths it was no perversion of the law. Robertson agrees that tithing itself is not condemned, and quotes the tale in the Talmud of a rabbi's ass so trained that it refused corn of which the tithes had not been taken.

The weightier matters are then defined. Calvin reads the closing clause as forestalling a calumny, since they might have charged him with making light of what God enjoined; he grants that no part of the law may be omitted, but holds that they overturn the natural order who begin with the smallest matters when the chief ones should have come first, the lesser being a kind of appendage, and that the commandments are so interwoven that none may be detached from the rest. Clarke takes the three words singly, judgment as equity toward all men, mercy as kindness to the distressed and miserable, and faith as trust in God as the fountain of righteousness, and says they neither began nor ended their works in God but did them to be seen of men and had their reward in human applause. Gill makes the contrast the hinge of the hypocrisy, strictness in trifling ceremonies that gained them credit alongside the neglect of internal religion. Henry holds that the weightiest commands are those most expressive of inward holiness, and suspects their niceness in tithing was meant to excuse the omission of these to men.

The proverb that follows raises a question about our own version. Barnes says the familiar wording is a misprint which leaves the verse without sense, the Greek meaning to strain a thing out through cloth or sieve, and explains the point by natural history, the gnat beginning as a grub in stagnant water which anyone nice about his drink would filter away. Clarke makes the same charge more precisely, that At stands for Out by an error of the press which escaped in the edition of 1611 and has been continued ever since, and produces older English Bibles which read strain out. Wesley adds that it is strange so glaring a false print should run through all the editions. Ellicott dissents, holding that there is scarcely evidence enough for the printer's blunder and that it is not probable in itself, and draws attention to what the two nouns have in common, the camel being named not merely as a vast thing but as an unclean beast forbidden for food. Robertson presses that common ground, the insect and the camel being ceremonially unclean, and quotes the rabbinic saying that he who kills a flea on the sabbath is as guilty as if he had killed a camel. Calvin states what the figure is for, the affected scrupulousness of men who shrink from a very small fault as though one transgression were more revolting than a hundred deaths while permitting themselves the most heinous crimes, which is as absurd as straining out a crumb and swallowing a whole loaf.
25:
The washed vessel is read as a charge about the source of what filled it. Clarke says they were exceedingly exact in the purifications the law prescribed and gave no attention to the inward purity those rites typified, and reports that the manuscripts offer a whole string of words for what the cup was full of, rapine, intemperance, injustice, uncleanness, covetousness and iniquity, remarking that if one puts them all together the character of the Pharisee will not be overcharged. Robertson treats the accusation as the gravest yet, these punctilious observers of ceremony not hesitating at robbery and graft, and calls it a picture of wickedness in high places both civil and ecclesiastical. Wesley finds the censure double, since they procured unjustly what they then used immoderately, so that luxury punished the fraud which fed it; and he widens the second word past eating and drinking to every immoderate desire, of honour or gain as much as of pleasure. Calvin puts the absurdity plainly, that it would be ridiculous to feast the eyes on outward splendour and then drink out of a cup full of dregs. Henry sharpens the same point, that the foolishness lies in washing the side which is only looked at and leaving dirty the side which is used. Barnes states the remedy as Christ gives it, that the vessel be filled with the fruits of honest industry, after which outside and inside will both be clean; and Ellicott adds that the outside named here includes the inner surface, so that contents pure in their source and their use make the whole clean without any washing of the surface at all.

The second figure is explained from the practice behind it. Lightfoot distinguishes the two kinds the rabbis knew, the deep grave that cannot be recognised and the painted one that is meant to be seen, observes that our Lord uses the first in the other Gospel and the second here, and quotes the tradition that on the fifteenth of Adar they repaired the roads and the sewers and marked the graves, the manner being to paint them with chalk tempered in water. Ellicott gives the reason, that contact brought ceremonial defilement, so the warning was annual and public, as a leper warned passers-by with his own cry, and notes that the word means smeared with lime powder. Robertson places them exactly, the graves of the poor in the fields and by the roadside rather than the rock-hewn tombs of the well-to-do, freshly done a month before the passover. Calvin treats the metaphor as the same lesson in another form, since a tomb built with beauty and splendour draws the eyes of men while inwardly it holds a stinking carcass.

The application names the appearance and what lies under it. Gill gathers up the whole chapter in it, the broadened phylacteries, the enlarged borders, the long prayers, the sea and land compassed for a proselyte, the tithed herbs and the scoured cup, as the several things by which they looked outwardly beautiful. Lightfoot supplies the Jewish name for such men, the distained or coloured, and the deathbed warning of Jannai the king to his wife to beware of painted men pretending to be Pharisees, whose works are the works of Zimri while they expect the reward of Phineas; they had forgotten, he adds, their own maxim that a disciple of the wise who is not the same within as without is no disciple at all. Ellicott cites the same warning independently and corrects the last word of the verse, which is better rendered lawlessness, a reckless disregard of the very law they professed to interpret. Clarke turns it on the reader, asking what the fair reputation acquired among men will avail when God sits in judgment upon the soul, and answering that a profession of holiness only sinks a man the deeper.
29:
What the tomb-building was for is disputed at once. Calvin rejects the reading that takes it for superstition in honouring the dead with splendid monuments, since they had not yet reached that pitch of blindness, and finds instead a bid for the favour of the ignorant multitude: by cherishing the memory of the prophets they passed for faithful imitators of them and keen zealots for the worship of God. Barnes keeps the plainer sense, that the sepulchres were raised professedly out of veneration, as men in the East still build a tomb to honour a distinguished name, so that in building them they professed to approve the prophets and to condemn their own fathers. Ellicott points to four conspicuous monuments still standing at the base of the Mount of Olives, whose mixture of debased Doric and Egyptian work belongs to the Herodian period, and suggests these may be the sepulchres meant. Robertson adds that some of the four may have been going up at the very hour Jesus spoke, and observes that in this last woe he addresses the nation and not the Pharisees only. Henry calls the whole business the varnish, and contrasts it with the older reverence of the king who thought it respect enough to leave a prophet's bones unmoved.

The profession that follows is weighed for sincerity. Ellicott sees no need to assume that they did not mean what they said, taking it for the unconscious hypocrisy of which every generation is guilty when it condemns the bigotry or greed of the past and then yields to the same sins itself. Clarke allows that they thought themselves much better than their ancestors, and turns the mirror round: many suppose that had they lived then they would not have done as those men did, which is hard to believe of people who reject the gospel and hate its followers now. Barnes puts the weight of the next verse on the two words unto yourselves, making it an appeal to conscience, since under all the profession they knew that they approved in their hearts the deed they disowned with their lips. Wesley presses the same charge through their own words, that by smooth speech as much as by cruel action they testify themselves the genuine sons of men who killed the prophets of their own time while venerating those of past ages. Calvin finds a double folly, that the honour paid to the dead was treated as a kind of expiation for the fathers' guilt, and that men descended from the bloody enemies of God should boast of a sacred ancestry.

The command to fill up the measure is taken four ways. Barnes reads it as prediction, a statement of what they were about to do, and completes the sense from what follows, that by slaying him they would make the national guilt full. Clarke reaches the same result by grammar, the imperative standing for the future after a Hebrew idiom, as when the temple is bidden be destroyed. Wesley hears permission rather than command, as though Christ said that he would contend with them no longer but leave them to the devices of their own hearts. Robertson calls it the keenest irony, and notes that some manuscripts have softened it into a plain future. Calvin denies that they are bidden do anything, and reads the words figuratively, that this cruelty is the ancient discipline of the nation, almost natural to them, so that they must be left to finish the web their fathers began. Gill supplies the measure itself, the bounds set to a nation's sin, which their fathers had carried far and which these sons would fill brimful by crucifying the Son of God. On the closing words Robertson, who finds that these blistering words cut like whip-cords, quotes a curse of the same shape from the Talmud upon the house of Annas.
34:
The sending is read as a strange sequel to the sentence just passed. Henry remarks on the connection, that after calling them a brood of vipers one would expect him to say they should never have a prophet again, whereas he says therefore he will send them prophets, either that they may yet be wrought upon or that they may be left inexcusable; and he notes that the sending is itself a claim, since to gift and commission prophets is an act of kingly office. Wesley hears the same claim in the bare words and distinguishes the three titles, prophets as men with supernatural credentials, wise men as those having natural ability and experience, and scribes as men of learning, adding that none of it would avail. Clarke identifies them with the evangelists, apostles and deacons who were to equal the ancient prophets in the gifts of the Spirit, and reads the threat precisely: some they would kill by legal process and some they would try and find guilty and hand to the Romans, who through them would put the men to death. Barnes names the fulfilments, Stephen killed and James, the scourging recorded in the Acts and by the apostle himself, and observes that the Jews had no power of crucifixion but gave their victims into Roman hands.

The reckoning of blood raises a question of identity. Lightfoot argues at length for the Zacharias killed by king Joash, on the grounds that no other of the name is said to have been slain before these words were spoken, that his death in the temple is related in express words, and that the Jews made it memorable by a signal revenge. Ellicott states the difficulty against that view, since the man stoned in the court of the house of the Lord was the son of Jehoiada, while the only son of Barachias in the older books is the minor prophet, of whose death nothing is known and whose murder in such a manner would hardly have gone unrecorded; he adds that the earlier death had gathered legends, the Talmud saying that the blood would not dry up. Robertson accepts the usual identification and admits the rest frankly, that how the words son of Barachiah entered this Gospel we do not know, and that half a dozen possibilities may be suggested. Henry begins the tally where the text does, with Abel, and finds it striking that the first man to die died for his religion.

Whether the children may be charged with the fathers' guilt is faced directly. Calvin grants the objection and answers it by conspiracy: since the whole nation through every age is involved in one rebellion, it is not strange that the punishment owed to the fathers should fall on the children. Barnes draws the distinction more narrowly, that God did not hold them guilty of what their fathers did, but that temporal judgments descend on children through a parent's wickedness, as a drunken father wastes the property his children might have had; the crimes being national, the judgment would be national, in the ruin of temple and city. Ellicott makes the imputation depend on the imitation, men making the guilt of past ages their own and reproducing its atrocities until what looks like an arbitrary decree becomes a righteous judgment, while repentance would cut off the entail. Henry says the same in his own figure, that patience abused turns into the greatest wrath, and the longer the treasures of wickedness are heaped up the fuller the treasures of wrath will be. Clarke fixes the phrase at the end on the race of men then living, a sense the word often carries in the Gospels, and Barnes dates the fulfilment about forty years from the speaking. Gill marks the solemn preface as the usual form for raising attention to something of moment.
37:
The lament is read first for its tone. Calvin says the city God had chosen for his own habitation had shown itself unworthy of the honour and, like a den of robbers, had grown accustomed to suck the blood of the prophets, the repeated name marking an impiety that deserves no ordinary detestation, and the charge being not one murder or two but a custom deeply rooted. Gill takes the address to fall not on the buildings but on the inhabitants, and among these chiefly on the rulers and the great council, since it belonged to them to examine men who claimed to be prophets and to condemn those they judged false. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew form of the name stands here only in this Gospel, as though the very syllables had fixed themselves in men's memories, and that the verbs are present, taking in the past and the future together, with a sad foresight of what lay in store for his own messengers. Henry sets the two occasions side by side, that a day or two before he had wept over the city and now he sighed over it, and plays on the name, the vision of peace becoming the seat of war and confusion. Lightfoot supplies what the rabbis themselves said of the city's record, that it had killed Uriah and Zechariah and Isaiah.

The figure of the hen is where the comment grows warmest. Clarke draws a doctrine from it, that our Lord seriously wished the salvation of these people and did everything which could be done consistently with his own perfections and the liberty of his creatures, his tears over the city proving his sincerity, so that if they perished the reason was their refusal to be gathered; from which he concludes that there have been men whom Christ wished to save and bled to save, who perished because they would not come to him. He adds the natural picture, the hen calling her chickens together at the sight of a bird of prey that she may cover them with her wings. Robertson renders the clause more exactly, how often did I long to gather them to myself, notes that the verb is the one used of the hen with her brood, and observes that the words imply earlier visits to the city such as the fourth Gospel records. Henry presses what the wings are for, protection and safety on the one hand and warmth and comfort on the other, so that souls have in Christ both refuge and refreshment.

The house is then given away, and the parting word disputed. Clarke and Wesley agree on the first point, that the temple which had been the Lord's own house is now called theirs to intimate that God had abandoned it, Wesley adding that it was spoken as he went out of it for the last time. Calvin explains the confidence that made the threat incredible to them, that they thought God bound to the place he had chosen for his only habitation in the world and treated the temple as an invincible fortress, as if they dwelt in the bosom of God. On the last verse Barnes holds that the day of mercy is gone by until the judgments have been borne, but that the days will come when the long-rejected nation will hail Jesus as the Messiah. Ellicott refers the welcome to the second Advent and to the true Israel of God, holding that for that generation and for the outward Israel the abandonment was final. Calvin rejects both the reading that defers everything to the last judgment and the reading that finds the words fulfilled soon after, and takes them of men who will find their Judge in the Redeemer they despised, and who even now sing that very psalm daily while scorning him whom it names.
